Session 7 · Matt’s skills · 03
mattpocock/skills
A skill encodes one good habit
An agent is only as good as the process you give it. A skill makes it run the same process every time.
terminal
$ npx skills@latest add mattpocock/skills
# or as a managed Claude Code plugin
$ claude plugins install mattpocock-skills
$ npx skills update # keep them fresh
Plain files. MIT licensed, 27 skills, works in Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and Copilot.
The problem
Left to guess, an agent writes plausible code that slowly rots the codebase.
The fix
One skill holds one habit: grill a plan, write a spec, review a diff.
Why it compounds
Each skill’s output is the next one’s input. Tune one step and the whole chain improves.
Plug-in solution
Skill

Session 7 · Matt’s skills · 05
The main flow
From idea to merged PR in six skills
Step 1
/grill-with-docs
Interviews you about the plan and records the decisions.
Step 2
/to-spec
Turns the agreed conversation into a written spec.
Step 3
/to-tickets
Splits the spec into small tickets an agent can build.
Step 4
/implement
One ticket, test-first. Or /implement-spec: all of them, in parallel.
Step 5
/code-review
Reviews the diff against your standards and against the spec.
Step 6
/retro
Looks back on the session and suggests fixes to the agent’s setup.
Branches: /prototype when only running code can answer · skip spec + tickets for one-session builds.

Session 7 · Matt’s skills · 07
Close calls
Look-alike skills split on one concrete test
/grill-me vs /grill-with-docs
Are you inside a working directory?
Yes → /grill-with-docs, so decisions land in the repo.
No → /grill-me, a plain alignment interview.
/grill-with-docs vs /wayfinder
Does the effort fit in one session?
Yes → /grill-with-docs.
No → /wayfinder: chart it as a map of decisions first.
/implement vs /implement-spec
One ticket, or the whole spec?
Yes → One ticket → /implement, test-first.
No → Whole task graph → /implement-spec, parallel subagents.
spec + tickets vs skip them
Does the build span more than one session?
Yes → /to-spec, then /to-tickets.
No → Skip both. The split isn’t worth its cost.
Session 7 · Matt’s skills · 08
Context management
Decide about context only at a phase boundary
Mid-phase, keep going. Between phases (grilling, building, QA), walk this list top to bottom.
1
Continue
The next phase needs this one verbatim, or you still have room. Rule it out first.
2
/clear
Everything behind you is disposable. Cheapest, and you can’t undo it.
3
/handoff
Something has to travel: a new harness, directory or colleague.
4
Subagent
The task is scoped tightly enough to run while you’re away.
5
/compact
None of the above. The default, so it comes last, not first.
Common mistake: /handoff is not the general way to change context windows. It only buys portability.
Session 7 · Matt’s skills · 09
From real use
Three gotchas before you roll it out
Gotcha 1
“Half the skills aren’t installed”
16 of the 27 skills set disable-model-invocation: true, so the agent’s skill list hides them. They are there. Type the slash command anyway.
Gotcha 2
“That skill does X”
/ask-matt answers from one-line summaries, not the skill itself. Before you act on its claim, ask it to open that SKILL.md.
Gotcha 3
“Just edit the SKILL.md”
npx skills update overwrites your edit and the plugin is read-only. Put standing rules in CLAUDE.md or say them in the prompt.
Rule: where the router and a SKILL.md disagree, the SKILL.md is right.

Graphify-Labs/graphify
Query a graph instead of grepping files

output
graphify-out/
├─ graph.html click, filter, search
├─ GRAPH_REPORT.md key concepts, surprises
└─ graph.json query without re-reading
Local, no LLM
Code is parsed with tree-sitter. Nothing leaves your machine.
Every edge explained
Each link is tagged EXTRACTED or INFERRED.
Not a vector index
No embeddings. A real graph you traverse.
Beyond code
~40 languages, plus docs, PDFs, images and video.

Topic 05
A code review agent that wants “code judo”
Cursor’s thermo-nuclear review skill, then the /code-review-plus flow I run on every branch.
Session 7 · Code review · 19
cursor/plugins · cursor-team-kit
It reviews structure, not style
SKILL.md · cursor/plugins
---
name: thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review
description: Run an extremely strict
maintainability review for abstraction
quality, giant files, and spaghetti-
condition growth. …
disable-model-invocation: true
---
The core ask
Audit the branch’s changes. Restructure for clarity without changing behaviour. Be ambitious: delete complexity, don’t move it.
What it reports first
Structural regressions, then missed simplifications, then spaghetti growth, boundaries, file size and legibility.
How it talks
A few high-conviction comments. No flood of cosmetic nits.
Plug-in solution
Skill
Session 7 · Code review · 20
Approval bar
Six things it blocks unless you can justify them
“It works” is not enough to approve. These are presumptive blockers.
Rule 1
No file past 1,000 lines
A PR that pushes a file over 1k lines needs a very strong reason. Decompose first.
Rule 2
No spaghetti growth
New one-off ifs in unrelated flows are a design problem, not a style nit.
Rule 3
Delete, don’t polish
Look for the move that makes whole branches, helpers or layers disappear.
Rule 4
Boring over magic
Flag thin wrappers, identity abstractions and pass-through helpers.
Rule 5
Clean type boundaries
Question any, unknown, casts and optionals that hide the real contract.
Rule 6
The canonical layer
Reuse the existing helper. Keep feature logic out of shared paths.

How to run it
Run it after the agent, before the merge
install in your repo
$ D=.claude/skills/thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review
$ mkdir -p $D
# copy SKILL.md from cursor/plugins into $D
> /thermo-nuclear-code-quality-review
Manual only. disable-model-invocation: true means Claude never runs it on its own. You type it when a diff is ready.
/code-review
Did we build the right thing? Matt’s skill: diff vs your standards and the spec.
/thermo-nuclear-…
Is this the simplest shape? Structure, abstractions, file size.
no-mistakes
Is it safe to open the PR? Review, tests and lint in a gate.
Session 7 · Code review · 22
My flow · /code-review-plus
This is the review flow I run on every branch
1
Know the intent first
Find acceptance criteria in docs/plans or the ticket. None? A helper subagent derives them.
2
Fan out in one message
Five blind reviewers get the diff + AC. A diagram agent draws the flow alongside.
3
Filter, then check tests
A challenge step keeps or discards every finding. Then tests are mapped to the change.
4
Score and publish
Severity + fix in chat, and the same data as an HTML report with a PNG of the flow.
Scale solution
Your own skill
Session 7 · Code review · 23
/code-review-plus · step by step
Eight steps, from diff to HTML report
Step 0
Gather diff
The branch’s changes saved as branch.diff.
Step 1
Find AC
From docs/plans or the ticket. None? A helper subagent derives them.
Step 2
Dispatch
One message: five blind reviewers get diff + AC, a diagram agent runs alongside.
Step 3
Challenge
Every finding is re-checked: keep or discard.
Step 4
Test coverage
List tests, map file → test, check fixtures, rank missing tests H/M/L.
Step 5
Score
Severity plus a concrete fix for each finding that survived.
Step 6
Chat report
Inline and scored, right in the session.
Step 7
HTML report
Findings, AC × tests, tests by file, missing tests, plus a PNG of the flow.

Step 2 · five blind reviewers
Five reviewers, one lens each, then a judge
Blind: no reviewer sees another’s findings, so none anchors on a wrong idea.
Correctness
Bugs, SSR, OWASP
Performance
O(n²), memory
Conventions
Style, Vue rules
Business logic
The diff vs each AC
Maintainability
Structure, simplicity
In
5 finding lists
Written independently, never shared between reviewers.
Step 3
Challenge
One agent judges every finding: keep or discard.
Step 5
Score
What survives gets a severity and a fix.
Plug in: thermo-nuclear rules into Maintainability, and Matt’s spec check into Business logic.
Session 7 · Code review · 25
Takeaways
Six habits of a reviewer agent worth trusting
01
Review against intent
Load the acceptance criteria first. Without them, it can only judge style.
02
One lens per agent
Narrow reviewers in parallel beat one agent asked to check everything.
03
Keep them blind
Independent reviewers don’t copy each other’s mistakes.
04
Challenge before you report
A second pass drops false positives, so people read fewer, better findings.
05
Tests are part of the review
Map every change to a test, then rank what’s missing.
06
Leave an artifact
Severity + fix in chat, and an HTML report and diagram for the team.
Why it matters: review becomes knowledge transfer. The report is how the team stays in charge.
Session 7 · Code review · 26
Topic 06
Will we write code again?
Kamil Mysliwiec, creator of NestJS · Trilon blog · 9 October 2026
Session 7 · Mindset · 27
trilon.io · Will we write code again?
The bottleneck moves from typing to attention
His view: agents now take a well-described task end to end. What stays with us are three jobs.
01
Decide
What to build, which stack, which trade-offs. Agents pick what was popular in their training data, not what fits your team.
02
Describe
What must change, what must not, how you know it’s done. Sometimes a signature or interface says it faster than words.
03
Verify
Tests, constraints, observability. If you don’t read every line, you need another way to see how it behaves.
“Typing was never the hard part.”
— Kamil Mysliwiec
Session 7 · Mindset · 28
trilon.io · Will we write code again?
What fades, and what matters more
Fading
Pair programming as two people, one keyboard
TDD as a hand-typed red-green ritual
DRY just in case, before duplication hurts
Line-by-line nitpick reviews of agent diffs
Matters more
Tests: how agents check their own work
Frameworks that enforce conventions, not suggest them
Observability: traces, logs, errors in production
Review as knowledge transfer: stay in charge
For juniors: still write code by hand on purpose. Judgement comes from fixing what you broke, like pilots who still fly manually.
